A mixture of anhydrous \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\) and conc. \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is called **Lucas** reagent. It converts an alcohol into an alkyl chloride, which does not dissolve and shows up as turbidity.

The reaction goes through a carbocation, and a tertiary carbocation is the most stable, so **tertiary** alcohols react fastest (turbidity at once). Secondary alcohols take about five minutes and primary alcohols show no turbidity at room temperature.

So the blanks are: **Lucas**, **tertiary**.

The cyanide ion is ambident: it can attack through carbon or through nitrogen.

\(\mathrm{KCN}\) is ionic, so the free \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) ion attacks through carbon and gives the nitrile:

\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl + KCN \xrightarrow{alc.} CH_3CN + KCl}\)

\(\mathrm{AgCN}\) is mainly covalent (the carbon is bonded to silver), so the lone pair on nitrogen attacks and the isocyanide forms:

\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl + AgCN \xrightarrow{alc.} CH_3NC + AgCl}\)

So the blanks are: **alc. KCN**, **alc. AgCN**.

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH}\)

Water is present in very large excess, so its concentration hardly changes during the reaction. The rate then depends only on the ester: rate \(= k'[\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5}]\). This makes the reaction **pseudo first order**.

The elementary step still needs one molecule of ester and one molecule of water to collide, so the molecularity is **two**.

So the blanks are: **first**, **two**.

A colligative property depends on the number of solute particles. When a solute dissociates, one formula unit gives two or more particles, so the van't Hoff factor \(i > 1\) and the colligative property becomes larger: an **increase**.

The molecular mass worked out from a colligative property is inversely proportional to that property (observed molar mass \(=\) normal molar mass \(/\,i\)), so the observed molecular mass shows a **decrease**.

So the blanks are: **increase**, **decrease**.

Phenol loses \(\mathrm{H^+}\) more readily than an aliphatic alcohol, so the assertion is true. The reason is that the negative charge of the phenoxide ion is spread over the benzene ring by resonance, which stabilises it. In an alkoxide ion the charge stays on oxygen (and alkyl groups push more electron density onto it), so there is no resonance stabilisation. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.

So the answer is option (A).

answers.value: Limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte = sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion
answers.working:
**Kohlrausch's Law of Independent Migration of ions:** at infinite dilution, when an electrolyte is completely dissociated, each ion moves independently of the other ions and makes its own definite contribution to the molar conductivity. So the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cations and anions:

\(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m} = \nu_{+}\lambda^{\infty}_{+} + \nu_{-}\lambda^{\infty}_{-}\)

where \(\nu_{+}\) and \(\nu_{-}\) are the numbers of cations and anions given by one formula unit of the electrolyte.

\(\mathrm{BaCl_2}\) gives one \(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions:

\(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{BaCl_2}) = \lambda^{\infty}(\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}) + 2\lambda^{\infty}(\mathrm{Cl^-}) = 127{\cdot}2 + 2 \times 76{\cdot}3 = 127{\cdot}2 + 152{\cdot}6 = 279{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\)

\(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{CaSO_4}) = \lambda^{\infty}(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}) + \lambda^{\infty}(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}) = 119{\cdot}0 + 160{\cdot}0 = 279{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\)

\(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{BaCl_2}) = 279{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\) (from part (ii)).

Increasing order: \(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{CaSO_4}) < \Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{BaCl_2})\), that is \(279{\cdot}0 < 279{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\).

answers.working:
**(i) Methyl magnesium bromide to propan-2-ol:** the Grignard reagent adds to acetaldehyde, and the addition product is hydrolysed with dilute acid.

\(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr + CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} (CH_3)_2CH{-}OMgBr}\)

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}OMgBr + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} (CH_3)_2CH{-}OH + Mg(OH)Br}\)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\) is propan-2-ol.

**(ii) Phenol to benzene:** phenol is distilled with zinc dust, which removes the oxygen.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + Zn \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_6H_6 + ZnO}\)

The product is benzene.

Zinc is the anode (oxidation) and tin is the cathode (reduction):

\(\mathrm{Zn(s) + Sn^{2+}(aq) \longrightarrow Zn^{2+}(aq) + Sn(s)}\), so \(n = 2\).

\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = (-0{\cdot}14) - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}62\,\mathrm{V}\)

\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -2 \times 96500 \times 0{\cdot}62 = -119660\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}} = -119{\cdot}66\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)

The negative value shows the cell reaction is spontaneous.

answers.value: (i) aniline + \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\)/HCl at 273-278 K gives benzene diazonium chloride; (ii) benzene diazonium chloride + CuCl/HCl gives chlorobenzene
answers.working:
**(i) Diazotisation reaction:** a primary aromatic amine reacts with nitrous acid (made in the mixture from \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\)) at 273 K to 278 K to give a diazonium salt.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2 + NaNO_2 + 2HCl \xrightarrow{273{-}278\,K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H_2O}\)

Aniline gives benzene diazonium chloride.

**(ii) Sandmeyer's reaction:** the diazonium group is replaced by \(\mathrm{{-}Cl}\), \(\mathrm{{-}Br}\) or \(\mathrm{{-}CN}\) using the corresponding copper(I) salt.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{CuCl\,/\,HCl} C_6H_5Cl + N_2}\)

Benzene diazonium chloride gives chlorobenzene. (Similarly, \(\mathrm{CuBr/HBr}\) gives bromobenzene and \(\mathrm{CuCN/KCN}\) gives benzonitrile.)

For a first order reaction, \(k =\dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]}\).

**Rate constant:** after 20 min the reaction is 40% complete, so 60% remains: \([\mathrm{A}]_0 / [\mathrm{A}] = 100/60\).

\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{20}\log\dfrac{100}{60} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{20} \times 0{\cdot}2218 = 0{\cdot}02554\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

**Time for 90% completion:** 10% remains, so \([\mathrm{A}]_0 / [\mathrm{A}] = 100/10 = 10\).

\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 10 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{0{\cdot}02554} \times 1 = 90{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{min}\)

The reaction takes about **90 minutes** to be 90% complete.

(Fehling's solution also works: acetaldehyde gives a red precipitate of \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\), acetone does not.)

**(b) Acetic acid and benzaldehyde: sodium bicarbonate test.** Add sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to each. Acetic acid gives brisk effervescence of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (which turns lime water milky). Benzaldehyde gives no effervescence.

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH + NaHCO_3 \longrightarrow CH_3COONa + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}\)

(Alternatively, benzaldehyde gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, while acetic acid does not.)

answers.value: (i) Zn has a stable fully filled \(\mathrm{3d^{10}4s^2}\) configuration and higher nuclear charge, while Cr loses its single 4s electron easily; (ii) \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) (pink/purple) is reduced to colourless \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) by oxalic acid
answers.working:
**(i)** Electronic configurations: Cr (24) \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^5 4s^1}\); Zn (30) \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{10} 4s^2}\).

In chromium, the first electron is removed from a singly occupied 4s orbital, and the ion left behind (\(\mathrm{3d^5}\)) is stable, so little energy is needed. In zinc, the electron must be taken from a completely filled 4s orbital of an extra-stable fully filled \(\mathrm{3d^{10}4s^2}\) configuration. Zinc also has a higher nuclear charge and a smaller atomic size, so its outer electrons are held more firmly. Hence the first ionisation enthalpy of Cr is less than that of Zn.

**(ii)** In acidic medium \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) is a strong oxidising agent. On warming it oxidises oxalic acid to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and is itself reduced from the coloured permanganate ion (Mn in +7 state) to the almost colourless \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ion, so the pink colour disappears.

\(\mathrm{2MnO_4^- + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^+ \longrightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O}\)

or \(\mathrm{2KMnO_4 + 3H_2SO_4 + 5(COOH)_2 \longrightarrow K_2SO_4 + 2MnSO_4 + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O}\)

answers.working:
**(i) Chlorobenzene to aniline:** chlorobenzene is heated with aqueous ammonia in the presence of cuprous oxide at about 475 K and 60 atm.

\(\mathrm{2C_6H_5Cl + 2NH_3 + Cu_2O \xrightarrow{475\,K,\ 60\,atm} 2C_6H_5NH_2 + 2CuCl + H_2O}\)

The product is aniline.

**(ii) Iodoform to acetylene:** iodoform is heated with silver powder, which removes the iodine atoms.

\(\mathrm{2CHI_3 + 6Ag \xrightarrow{\Delta} HC{\equiv}CH + 6AgI}\)

The product is acetylene (ethyne).

\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl + Mg \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} CH_3MgCl}\)

\(\mathrm{CH_3MgCl + HCHO \longrightarrow CH_3CH_2OMgCl \xrightarrow{H_2O/H^+} CH_3CH_2OH + Mg(OH)Cl}\)

The product is ethanol.

**(ii) Benzene diazonium chloride to phenol:** the diazonium salt is warmed with water (dilute acid); nitrogen is given off.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + H_2O \xrightarrow{warm} C_6H_5OH + N_2 + HCl}\)

The product is phenol.

**(iii) Sodium ethoxide to ethoxyethane (Williamson synthesis):** sodium ethoxide is heated with ethyl bromide.

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5ONa + C_2H_5Br \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5 + NaBr}\)

The product is ethoxyethane (diethyl ether).

\(\mathrm{H_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH + H_2N{-}CH(CH_3){-}COOH \longrightarrow H_2N{-}CH_2{-}CO{-}NH{-}CH(CH_3){-}COOH + H_2O}\)

**(iii)** Glucose is oxidised by a mild oxidising agent, bromine water, to gluconic acid, a six-carbon acid with the same carbon chain:

\(\mathrm{CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\ water} COOH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH}\)

Only an aldehyde group is oxidised this easily to a carboxylic acid without loss of carbon, so the carbonyl group in glucose is an aldehyde (\(\mathrm{{-}CHO}\)) group. A sugar with an aldehyde group is an aldose, so glucose is an aldose (an aldohexose). (Glucose also reduces Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution, which supports the same conclusion.)

**(a)** By Kohlrausch's law:

\(\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \lambda^{\infty}_{\mathrm{H^+}} + \lambda^{\infty}_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}} = 348{\cdot}65 + 41{\cdot}4 = 390{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda^{c}_{m}}{\Lambda^{\infty}_{m}} = \dfrac{40{\cdot}65}{390{\cdot}05} = 0{\cdot}104\)

So acetic acid is about \(10{\cdot}4\%\) dissociated at this concentration.

**(b)** **[B]** is the weak electrolyte. A strong electrolyte is already almost fully ionised, so on dilution its molar conductivity rises only slightly (because the ions are freer to move), as with [A]. A weak electrolyte is only slightly ionised; dilution greatly increases its degree of dissociation and hence the number of ions, so its molar conductivity rises steeply, as with [B] (30 times).

**(c)** **No**, copper sulphate cannot be stored in a zinc pot. Zinc has a lower (more negative) reduction potential than copper, so zinc is a stronger reducing agent and will displace copper from the solution:

\(\mathrm{Zn(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \longrightarrow ZnSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)}\)

\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = 0{\cdot}34 - (-0{\cdot}76) = +1{\cdot}10\,\mathrm{V}\)

The positive \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\) shows the reaction is spontaneous, so the pot would dissolve and copper would deposit.

answers.working:
**(a)** Charge passed: \(Q = I \times t = 0{\cdot}75 \times 25 \times 60 = 1125\,\mathrm{C}\)

At the cathode: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \longrightarrow Cu}\), so 2 F (\(2 \times 96500\,\mathrm{C}\)) deposit one mole (atomic weight \(M\) grams) of copper.

\(m = \dfrac{M \times Q}{2F}\), so \(M = \dfrac{m \times 2F}{Q} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}370 \times 2 \times 96500}{1125} = \dfrac{71410}{1125} = 63{\cdot}48\)

The atomic weight of copper is about **\(63{\cdot}5\)**.

**(b)** **Metal A** liberates \(\mathrm{H_2}\). Its standard reduction potential (\(-0{\cdot}76\,\mathrm{V}\)) is lower than that of the hydrogen electrode (\(0{\cdot}00\,\mathrm{V}\)), so A is a stronger reducing agent than hydrogen and can reduce \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions:

\(\mathrm{A + 2H^+ \longrightarrow A^{2+} + H_2\uparrow}\) (for example \(\mathrm{Zn + H_2SO_4 \longrightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2}\))

Metal B (\(+0{\cdot}34\,\mathrm{V}\)) lies above hydrogen and cannot reduce \(\mathrm{H^+}\), so it gives no hydrogen.

**(c)** Specific conductivity is the conductance of one unit volume (1 \(\mathrm{cm^3}\)) of the solution, so it depends on the number of ions present in that volume. On dilution the total number of ions is spread over a larger volume, so the number of ions per \(\mathrm{cm^3}\) falls and \(\kappa\) decreases (even though the degree of dissociation may increase).

answers.working:
**(i)** \(\Delta T_f = 1{\cdot}5\,\mathrm{K}\), \(K_f = 3{\cdot}9\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}\), \(M_2 = 176\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\), \(w_1 = 75\,\mathrm{g}\).

\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{K_f \times w_2 \times 1000}{M_2 \times w_1}\), so \(w_2 = \dfrac{\Delta T_f \times M_2 \times w_1}{K_f \times 1000} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 \times 176 \times 75}{3{\cdot}9 \times 1000} = \dfrac{19800}{3900} = 5{\cdot}08\,\mathrm{g}\)

About **\(5{\cdot}08\,\mathrm{g}\)** of ascorbic acid must be dissolved.

**(ii)** Moles of solute: \(n = \dfrac{6{\cdot}8}{321{\cdot}45} = 0{\cdot}02115\,\mathrm{mol}\)

Volume \(V = 0{\cdot}1\,\mathrm{L}\), \(T = 25 + 273 = 298\,\mathrm{K}\), \(R = 0{\cdot}0821\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\).

\(\pi = \dfrac{n}{V}RT = \dfrac{0{\cdot}02115}{0{\cdot}1} \times 0{\cdot}0821 \times 298 = 0{\cdot}2115 \times 24{\cdot}47 = 5{\cdot}18\,\mathrm{atm}\)

The osmotic pressure is about **\(5{\cdot}18\,\mathrm{atm}\)** (with \(R = 0{\cdot}083\ \mathrm{L\,bar\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\) it is about \(5{\cdot}23\,\mathrm{bar}\)).

**(iii)** Aquatic animals breathe the oxygen dissolved in water. The solubility of a gas in a liquid falls as temperature rises: dissolving a gas is exothermic, and the Henry's law constant \(K_H\) increases with temperature, so at a given partial pressure less gas dissolves (\(p = K_H x\)). Cold water therefore holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water, which is why aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water.

answers.working:
**(i)(a)** Dry distillation of calcium acetate gives acetone (propanone):

\(\mathrm{(CH_3COO)_2Ca \xrightarrow{dry\ distillation} CH_3COCH_3 + CaCO_3}\)

**(i)(b)** Zinc amalgam and conc. HCl reduce the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group to \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}\) (Clemmensen reduction), so acetaldehyde gives ethane:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + 4[H] \xrightarrow{Zn/Hg,\ conc.\ HCl} CH_3CH_3 + H_2O}\)

**(i)(c)** Esterification: acetic acid and ethyl alcohol form ethyl acetate (a sweet smelling ester) and water:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH \overset{conc.\ H_2SO_4}{\rightleftharpoons} CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

**(ii)** \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O}\) that is easily oxidised and gives the haloform reaction must be acetaldehyde, which has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO{-}}\) group. This is confirmed by the HCN reaction:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + HCN \longrightarrow CH_3CH(OH)CN}\) ([Z], 2-hydroxypropanenitrile)

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CN + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3CH(OH)COOH + NH_3}\) (2-hydroxypropanoic acid, lactic acid)

**(a)** [X] is acetaldehyde (ethanal), \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CHO}\). On oxidation it gives [Y], acetic acid (ethanoic acid), \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}COOH}\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{[O]} CH_3COOH}\)

Haloform reaction of [X]: \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \longrightarrow CHI_3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H_2O}\)

**(b)** With dilute NaOH, acetaldehyde undergoes aldol condensation. The product is **3-hydroxybutanal (aldol)**:

\(\mathrm{2CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\)

(On heating, aldol loses water to give but-2-enal, crotonaldehyde.)

answers.value: (a) +3; paramagnetic; 3 unpaired; \(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\); (b) P \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5NO_2]Cl}\), Q \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]NO_2}\), ionisation isomerism; (c) \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) does not release free \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions
answers.working:
**(a)** In \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) is neutral, so:

**(1)** the oxidation number of chromium is **+3**.

Cr (24): \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^5 4s^1}\); \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\): \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^3}\). The three d electrons occupy three of the five 3d orbitals singly, leaving two 3d orbitals empty. These two 3d, one 4s and three 4p orbitals hybridise and accept six lone pairs from six \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) molecules.

**(2)** The complex is **paramagnetic**.

**(3)** It has **3 unpaired electrons** (\(\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3{\cdot}87\) BM).

**(4)** The hybridisation is **\(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\)** (inner orbital octahedral complex).

**(b)(1)** Isomer P gives a white precipitate of AgCl, so its chloride is outside the coordination sphere as a free ion. Isomer Q gives no precipitate, so its chloride is bound to cobalt and the nitrite ion is outside.

P: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl}\), pentaamminenitrito-N-cobalt(III) chloride

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl + AgNO_3 \longrightarrow [Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]NO_3 + AgCl\downarrow}\) (white)

Q: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]NO_2}\), pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) nitrite

**(b)(2)** The two compounds give different ions in solution, so this is **ionisation isomerism**.

**(c)** Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II), \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\), is a complex compound, not a double salt. In water it ionises only as:

\(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6] \longrightarrow 4K^+ + [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\)

The \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion is held firmly inside the very stable complex ion by six strong field \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) ligands and is not set free. Since there are no free \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions in the solution, the test for the ferrous ion is not given.

**(a)**

**(1)** \(\mathrm{d^4}\), high spin octahedral (weak field, \(\Delta_o <\) pairing energy): the fourth electron goes into \(\mathrm{e_g}\) rather than pairing. Configuration: \(\mathrm{t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1}\).

**(2)** \(\mathrm{d^6}\), low spin octahedral (strong field, \(\Delta_o >\) pairing energy): all six electrons pair up in \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\). Configuration: \(\mathrm{t_{2g}^6\,e_g^0}\).

**(b)** In an octahedral field each \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) electron lowers the energy by \(0{\cdot}4\Delta_o\) and each \(\mathrm{e_g}\) electron raises it by \(0{\cdot}6\Delta_o\):

CFSE \(= (-0{\cdot}4\,x + 0{\cdot}6\,y)\Delta_o\), where \(x\) and \(y\) are the numbers of \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) and \(\mathrm{e_g}\) electrons.

**(1)** \(\mathrm{t_{2g}^3e_g^1}\): CFSE \(= (-0{\cdot}4 \times 3 + 0{\cdot}6 \times 1)\Delta_o = (-1{\cdot}2 + 0{\cdot}6)\Delta_o = -0{\cdot}6\Delta_o\)

**(2)** \(\mathrm{t_{2g}^6e_g^0}\): CFSE \(= (-0{\cdot}4 \times 6)\Delta_o = -2{\cdot}4\Delta_o\) (pairing energy ignored)

**(c)**

**(1)** \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5NO_2]Cl_2}\): the ambidentate \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\) ligand is bonded through oxygen in one and through nitrogen in the other. This is **linkage isomerism**.

**(2)** \(\mathrm{[PtCl_2(NH_3)_4]Br_2}\) and \(\mathrm{[PtBr_2(NH_3)_4]Cl_2}\): the ligand inside the sphere and the counter ion outside are exchanged, so they give different ions in solution (\(\mathrm{Br^-}\) in one, \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) in the other). This is **ionisation isomerism**.

**(d)** \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) is the outer orbital complex.

In both complexes iron is \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^6}\).

\(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is a weak field ligand, so the 3d electrons do not pair up: four of them stay unpaired and no inner 3d orbital is free. The six water lone pairs go into the 4s, three 4p and two 4d orbitals, giving \(\mathrm{sp^3d^2}\) hybridisation. Using the outer 4d orbitals makes it an **outer orbital (high spin) complex**, paramagnetic with 4 unpaired electrons.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\), \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) is a strong field ligand. It forces the six 3d electrons to pair in three orbitals, freeing two inner 3d orbitals, so the hybridisation is \(\mathrm{d^2sp^3}\): an inner orbital (low spin), diamagnetic complex.
